title: Kota
author: Chef Sipho
desc: A hollowed quarter loaf toasted, then packed with cheese, hot chips, split Russian sausage, a thickened tomato relish and two kinds of atchar — Gauteng's answer to a whole meal in bread.
longDesc: Kota is from the English quarter, and in Pretoria it is a spatlo and in the Vaal a skhambane. The build has a logic: cheese goes in first so it melts against the hot bread, chips next for bulk, then the protein, then the sauce, and the atchar last so its sharpness is not cooked away. Whether the kota or Durban's bunny chow came first is argued in both cities and no one has the evidence to settle it. This version tightens the sauce and toasts the bread, which most street kotas do not, and is the better for it.
ingredients: 2 x 700 g unsliced white loaves, quartered and hollowed
1 x 410 g tin tomato-and-onion braai relish
1 x 200 g punnet rosa or cherry tomatoes
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
8 smoked Russian sausages, or any sausage
2 x 150 g packets sliced mature Cheddar
steps: Hollow out each quarter loaf and toast both the soft inner piece and the crust at 180C for 5 to 10 minutes.
Simmer the braai relish with the Peppadews and the rosa tomatoes over medium heat for 10 to 15 minutes, until thickened, adding the sliced red peppers for the last 3 or 4 minutes.
Mix the two atchars together and set aside.
Cut the potatoes into fingers — thicker is better — heat the oil to 180C and deep-fry until golden. Drain on paper and toss with salt and pepper.
Roast the sausages until the skins are crisp, then slice each one lengthways.
Assemble in order: a sheet of cheese in the base of each quarter, then hot chips, then sausage, then sauce, then more cheese, and finally the atchar.
Add a small handful of microgreens and cap it with the toasted cut-out bread as a lid, just before serving.
chefTips: Cheese first, against the hot bread. It melts into the base and seals it against the sauce.
Atchar last, on top, uncooked. Its whole job is sharpness and heat is the enemy of that.
Thick-cut chips. Thin ones collapse under the sauce within a minute.
Assemble to order. A kota that has stood for ten minutes is a different and worse thing.
The street version usually skips the toasting and uses whatever is in the fridge — polony, a vienna, a fried egg, a slice of liver. All of it is correct.
commonMistakes: Putting the sauce in before the cheese, so the bread goes through.
Building them in advance for a crowd — they do not hold.
storage: Not a keeping dish. The components keep 2 days separately.
reheating: Reheat the components and build a fresh kota.
healthBenefits: Substantial protein from the sausage and cheese.
The atchar and the raw greens add vitamin C to an otherwise cooked plate.
It is designed to be filling and cheap, and it succeeds at both.
culturalNote: The kota is informal-economy food and one of the most widespread food businesses in Gauteng, sold from spaza shops and corner stands. The late Lesego Semenya, who wrote Dijo, did more than anyone to get township cooking taken seriously as cooking rather than as sociology, and this chef-style build is his.
